247: I am not alone in being unfortunate.
All men are disappointed in their hopes and deceived in their expectations.
I have paid a visit to my good old woman under the lime-trees.
The eldest boy ran out to meet me; his shout of joy brought out his mother, but she had a very melancholy look.
Her first words were, "Alas, dear sir, my little John is dead."
He was the youngest of her children.
"And my husband has come back from Switzerland without any money; if some kind people had not helped him, he would have had to beg his way home."
"He was taken ill with a fever on the journey."
I could find nothing to answer, and made the little one a present.
She asked me to take some fruit; I did, and left the place with a sorrowful heart.
249: Sometimes a happy prospect opens before me — but alas, only for a moment.
And then, lost in reverie, I cannot help saying to myself: "If Albert were to die? Yes — she would become — and I should be —"
And so I chase a chimera, until it leads me to the edge of a precipice and I shudder.
250: When I pass through the same gate and walk along the same road that first brought me to Charlotte, my heart sinks at the change that has come since.
No sentiment, no beat of my heart is the same.

I feel as some departed prince might feel, whose spirit came back to visit the superb palace he had built in happy times, adorned with costly magnificence and left to a beloved son — and who found its glory gone and its halls deserted and in ruins.
252: Sometimes I cannot understand how she can love another, how she dares love another, when I love nothing in this world so completely and so devotedly as I love her, when I know nothing but her and have nothing else in the world.
254: As nature puts on her autumn colours, it becomes autumn in me and around me.
My leaves are dry and yellow, and the trees nearby are stripped of theirs.
Do you remember my writing to you about a peasant boy shortly after I arrived here?
I have just been asking after him in Walheim.
They say he has been dismissed from his service, and is now avoided by everyone.
I met him yesterday on the road, walking to a neighbouring village.
I spoke to him, and he told me his story.
It interested me enormously, as you will easily understand when I repeat it to you.
But why should I trouble you?
Why should I not keep all my sorrow to myself?
Why should I go on giving you occasion to pity me and blame me?
But no matter; this too is part of my destiny.
255: At first the peasant lad answered my questions with a kind of subdued melancholy, which seemed to me the mark of a timid nature.
But as we came to understand each other he spoke with less reserve, confessed his faults openly, and lamented his misfortune.
I wish, my dear friend, I could give his words their proper force.

He told me, with a kind of pleasure in the memory, that after I left, his passion for his mistress grew daily, until at last he knew neither what he did nor what he said nor what was to become of him.
He could neither eat nor drink nor sleep; he felt as if he were suffocating; he disobeyed every order and forgot every command without meaning to.
He seemed pursued by an evil spirit, until one day, knowing that his mistress had gone up to an upper room, he followed her — or rather was drawn after her.
As she was deaf to his entreaties, he resorted to force.

He does not know what happened; but he called God to witness that his intentions toward her were honourable, and that he wished for nothing more sincerely than that they should marry and spend their lives together.
When he had got this far he began to hesitate, as though there were something he had not the courage to say.
At length he admitted, with some confusion, certain little confidences she had encouraged, and liberties she had allowed.
He broke off two or three times in the telling, and assured me most earnestly that he had no wish to make her out bad, as he put it, for he still loved her as sincerely as ever.
He said the tale had never passed his lips before, and that he told it now only to convince me that he was not utterly lost and abandoned.
And here, my dear friend, I must begin the old song you know I am for ever singing.
If I could only show you the man as he stood, and as he stands now before me, if I could only give you his real words, you would be compelled to feel for his fate.
But enough: you, who know my misfortune and my disposition, can easily understand what draws me toward every unfortunate creature, and toward this one above all.
256: Reading this letter over a second time, I find I have left out the end of my tale; but it is easily supplied.
She grew reserved toward him at the prompting of her brother, who had long hated him and wanted him out of the house.
The brother feared that his sister's second marriage might rob his children of the handsome fortune they expect from her, since she is childless.
He was dismissed at last; and the whole affair caused so much scandal that the mistress dared not take him back, even if she had wished to.
She has since hired another servant, with whom, they say, her brother is equally displeased, and whom she is likely to marry.
But my informant assures me that he himself is determined not to survive such a catastrophe.
257: This story is neither exaggerated nor embellished.
Indeed I have weakened it and spoiled it in the telling, by having to use the more refined language of polite society.
258: So this love, this constancy, this passion, is no poetical fiction.
It is real, and it lives in its greatest purity among the class of people we call rude and uneducated.
We are the educated — the ones educated out of ourselves.
But read this story attentively, I implore you.
I am calm today, for I have been busy with this narration; you can see by my writing that I am not as agitated as usual.
I read this tale over and over, Wilhelm: it is the history of your friend.
My fortune has been and will be the same; and I am not half so brave nor half so determined as the poor wretch I hesitate to compare myself with.
260: Charlotte had written a letter to her husband in the country, where business was keeping him.
It began: "My dearest love, come back as soon as you can; I am waiting for you with a thousand raptures."
A friend arrived with word that for certain reasons he could not return at once.
Charlotte's letter was not sent on, and that same evening it fell into my hands.
"What a heavenly treasure the imagination is," I exclaimed. "For a moment I fancied this had been written to me."
262: It cost me a great deal to part with the blue coat I wore the first time I danced with Charlotte.
But I could not possibly wear it any longer.
I have ordered a new one exactly like it, down to the collar and the sleeves, and a new waistcoat and breeches as well.
263: But it does not have the same effect on me.
I do not know how it is; but I hope that in time I shall like it better.
265: She has been away for some days.
Today I visited her; she rose to receive me, and I kissed her hand most tenderly.
266: At that moment a canary flew from a mirror and settled on her shoulder.
"Here is a new friend," she said, making him perch on her hand. "He is a present for the children."
"When I feed him he flutters his wings and pecks so prettily."
267: She held the bird to her mouth, and he pressed her sweet lips with such fervour that he seemed to feel the excess of bliss he was enjoying.
268: "He shall kiss you too," she added, and held the bird toward me.
His little beak moved from her mouth to mine, and the delightful sensation seemed like the forerunner of the sweetest bliss.
269: "A kiss," I said, "does not seem to satisfy him: he wants food, and seems disappointed by these unsatisfying endearments."
270: "But he eats out of my mouth," she went on, and held out her lips to him with seed between them.
And she smiled with all the charm of a creature who has allowed an innocent share in her love.
271: She should not do such things.
She ought not to stir my imagination with these displays of heavenly innocence and happiness, nor wake my heart out of the sleep in which it dreams that life is worthless.
Because she knows how much I love her.
273: It makes me wretched, Wilhelm, to think that there should be people incapable of valuing the few things in life that are really worth anything.
You remember the walnut trees at S—, where I used to sit with Charlotte during my visits to the worthy old vicar.
Those glorious trees, the very sight of which so often filled my heart with joy!
How they adorned and refreshed the parsonage yard with their wide-spreading branches!
And how pleasant it was to remember the good old pastor who planted them with his own hands so many years ago.
The schoolmaster has often mentioned his name; he had it from his grandfather.
He must have been an excellent man, and under the shade of those old trees his memory was always sacred to me.
The schoolmaster told us yesterday, with tears in his eyes, that the trees had been felled.
Yes, cut to the ground!
In my rage I could have killed the monster who struck the first blow.
And I have to endure it — I, who if I had two such trees in my own yard and one of them died of old age, should weep with real grief.
But there is some comfort left: such a thing is sentiment.
The whole village murmurs at the loss; and I hope the vicar's wife will soon discover, from the drying up of the villagers' presents, how deeply she has wounded the feelings of the neighbourhood.
For it was she who did it — the wife of the present incumbent, our good old man being dead.
She is a tall, sickly creature, who is right enough to take no notice of the world, since the world takes no notice of her.

The silly being affects learning, pretends to examine the canonical books, lends her aid to the new-fashioned moral and critical reformation of Christendom, and shrugs her shoulders at the mention of Lavater's enthusiasm.
Her health is ruined, on account of which she is prevented from enjoying anything here below.
Only such a creature could have cut down my walnut trees.
I can never pardon it.
Hear her reasons.
The falling leaves made the yard wet and dirty; the branches shut out the light; boys threw stones at the nuts when they were ripe, and the noise affected her nerves.
It disturbed her profound meditations, when she was weighing the difficulties of Kennicot, Semler, and Michaelis.
Finding that the whole parish, and the old people especially, were displeased, I asked why they had allowed it.
"Ah, sir!" they answered, "when the steward orders a thing, what can we poor peasants do?"
But one thing has turned out well.
The steward and the vicar — who for once thought to get some advantage out of his wife's caprices — intended to divide the trees between them.
The revenue office, hearing of it, revived an old claim to the ground where the trees had stood, and sold them to the highest bidder.
There they still lie on the ground.
If I were the sovereign, I should know how to deal with the whole lot of them — vicar, steward, and revenue office.
Sovereign, did I say?
If I were, I should care little about the trees that grow in my country.
275: Only to look into her dark eyes is a source of happiness to me.
And what grieves me is that Albert does not seem as happy as he — hoped to be — as I should have been — if —
I am no friend to these dashes, but here I cannot put it otherwise; and I dare say I have made myself clear enough.
277: Ossian has driven Homer out of my heart.
What a world this glorious bard carries me into!
To wander over pathless wastes, surrounded by raging whirlwinds, where by the feeble light of the moon we see the spirits of our ancestors.

To hear from the mountain tops, above the roar of the torrents, their plaintive voices coming out of deep caves, and the sorrowful lament of a maiden who sighs out her life on the mossy tomb of the warrior she adored.
I meet this bard with his silver hair; he wanders in the valley, looking for the footsteps of his fathers, and finds, alas, only their graves.
Then, gazing at the pale moon as she sinks beneath the waves of the rolling sea, the hero's mind is struck by the memory of days gone by.
Days when approaching danger put strength into the brave, and the moon shone on his boat coming home in triumph, laden with spoils.

When I read deep sorrow in his face; when I see his dying glory sink exhausted into the grave, as he draws a new and heart-thrilling delight from the thought of being joined with his beloved; when he casts a look at the cold earth and the tall grass so soon to cover him, and then cries out:
"The traveller will come — he will come who has seen my beauty, and he will ask, 'Where is the bard, where is the illustrious son of Fingal?' He will walk over my tomb, and will look for me in vain!"

Then, O my friend, I could draw my sword that instant like a true and noble knight, and deliver my prince from the long and painful languor of a living death — and send my own soul after the demigod my hand had set free.
279: Alas, the void — the fearful void I feel in my breast!
Sometimes I think that if I could only once, just once, press her to my heart, this dreadful void would be filled.
281: Yes, I feel certain of it, Wilhelm, and every day more certain: the existence of any one creature is of very little consequence.
A friend of Charlotte's called to see her just now.
I withdrew into the next room and took up a book; but finding I could not read, I sat down to write.
I heard them talking in undertones; they spoke of indifferent things and passed on the news of the town.
One woman was going to be married; another was ill, very ill — she had a dry cough, her face was growing thinner daily, and she had fits from time to time.
"N— is very unwell too," said Charlotte.
"His limbs are beginning to swell already," answered the other; and my lively imagination carried me straight to the beds of the sick.
There I see them struggling against death, with all the agonies of pain and horror; and these women, Wilhelm, talk about it as indifferently as one might mention the death of a stranger.

And when I look round the room I am sitting in — when I see Charlotte's clothes lying before me, and Albert's papers, and all the furniture so familiar to me, down to the very inkstand I am using — when I think what I am to this family: everything.
My friends esteem me; I often add to their happiness; and my heart feels as though it could not beat without them.
And yet — if I were to die, if I were called away out of the middle of this circle, would they feel it, and for how long would they feel the void my loss would make in their lives?

Yes, such is the frailty of man, that even there, where he is most conscious of his own being, where he makes the strongest and most forcible impression — even in the memory and the heart of the woman he loves — even there he must perish and vanish, and quickly.
283: I could tear my breast open with vexation to think how little we are able to influence each other's feelings.

No one can give me the sensations of love, joy, rapture and delight that I do not naturally possess; and though my heart may glow with the liveliest affection, I cannot make happy anyone in whom that same warmth is not already there.
285: I possess so much, and my love for her swallows it all.
I possess so much, and without her I have nothing.
287: A hundred times I have been on the point of embracing her.
Heavens, what a torment it is to see so much loveliness passing back and forth in front of you, and not dare to lay a hand on it!
And laying hold is the most natural of human instincts.
Do children not touch everything they see?
